issues.legal_issue: A High Court should not determine the contractual merits of a cancellation and guarantee-invocation dispute in writ proceedings when resolving it requires examination of serious, disputed facts.
material_facts: A promoter undertook to submit project materials, obtain clearances and achieve financial closure, and provided a performance guarantee securing those obligations.
The project location changed, and the promoter later stated that it could not proceed at the alternative site because of site conditions.
The public authority cancelled the letter of intent and invoked the guarantee after treating the promoter’s non-performance as a breach.

The promoter challenged the cancellation and invocation in a writ petition, and the High Court addressed whether the cancellation and forfeiture were justified despite disputed questions about the project and performance.
issues.conclusion: The High Court should not have decided in the writ proceeding whether the cancellation was legally justified or whether the underlying circumstances excused the promoter’s non-performance; those matters involved disputed questions of fact and could be pursued in appropriate proceedings.
issues.legal_principle: Article 226 jurisdiction is discretionary and may be exercised in contractual matters, but, under the principles summarized in Joshi Technologies International Inc. v. Union of India (2015) 7 SCC 728, drawing on ABL International Ltd. v. Export Credit Guarantee Corporation of India Ltd. (2004) 3 SCC 553 and Whirlpool Corporation v. Registrar of Trade Marks (1998) 8 SCC 1, a court normally will not decide serious and complex factual disputes requiring evidence in writ proceedings. The existence of a contractual dispute does not invariably bar a writ, but writ jurisdiction is not intended to facilitate avoidance of voluntarily incurred contractual obligations.

predicates.contractual_writ_proceeding: A party brought writ proceedings seeking review of a public authority’s action arising from contractual obligations.
predicates.serious_disputed_facts: The dispute over performance or the authority’s action involved serious factual disagreements requiring detailed examination.

issues.definition: When a contractual dispute is brought in writ proceedings and its resolution involves serious disputed facts, the High Court does not decide the contractual merits in that proceeding.

issues.legal_issue: An unconditional bank guarantee may not be restrained from being honoured merely because the underlying parties dispute the contract, absent egregious fraud or irretrievable harm.
material_facts: A bank issued an unconditional guarantee providing that it would pay on the public authority’s written demand stating that the promoter had failed to perform its obligations.
The guarantee made the authority’s decision as to breach binding on the bank and required payment without demur, irrespective of disputes between the authority and the promoter.
The authority cancelled the letter of intent and made a written demand under the guarantee after deciding that the promoter had failed to perform.
The promoter sought a writ order restraining encashment, relying on its challenge to the cancellation and the underlying contractual dispute.
issues.conclusion: The guarantee was an independent contract between the bank and the beneficiary, and the bank was bound to honour a demand made in accordance with its terms; the High Court should not have restrained invocation on the basis of the underlying contractual dispute.
issues.legal_principle: An unconditional bank guarantee is an independent and separate contract, and disputes under the underlying contract do not ordinarily justify an injunction against its enforcement. Under Himadri Chemicals Industries Ltd. v. Coal Tar Refining Company (2007) 8 SCC 110, an injunction may be considered for egregious fraud that vitiates the guarantee’s foundation or where encashment would cause irretrievable harm or injustice. The guarantee’s terms governed the bank’s obligation to pay on the beneficiary’s demand.

rule.if: appeal_from_writ_injunction and unconditional_bank_guarantee and compliant_written_demand and not egregious_fraud and not irretrievable_harm

predicates.appeal_from_writ_injunction: An appeal concerns a writ order restraining a beneficiary from invoking a bank guarantee.
predicates.unconditional_bank_guarantee: A bank gave a guarantee requiring payment on demand without demur and treating the beneficiary’s determination of breach as binding on the bank.
predicates.compliant_written_demand: The beneficiary made a written demand in the manner required by the guarantee and stated that the underlying obligor had failed to perform.
predicates.egregious_fraud: The demand was made in circumstances involving fraud that vitiated the very foundation of the guarantee.
predicates.irretrievable_harm: Honouring the guarantee would cause harm or injustice that could not be remedied.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns an injunction against an unconditional guarantee, the beneficiary made a compliant written demand, and neither egregious fraud nor irretrievable harm is present, the injunction is denied.
